data: The original GNSS — 31 satellites, free public service since 2000
US Space Force GPS Operations. Originally a Department of Defense system; civilian unencrypted L1 C/A signal freely available worldwide.

Global Positioning System — the original GNSS and still the most widely used. 31 active satellites at 20,180 km in 6 orbital planes inclined 55°. Operated by US Space Force; originally Department of Defense. President Reagan's 1983 directive promised future civilian GPS access after the Korean Air Lines 007 shootdown, but civilian unencrypted L1 C/A signal access was not available until Selective Availability was turned off in May 2000, dramatically improving civilian accuracy. Modernised L1C, L2C, L5 signals on Block IIF and III satellites.
US early-warning IR sensors hosted on classified Tundra-orbit platforms
NOAA geostationary weather pair — Americas continuous coverage
Russia's GNSS — 24 sats, restored to full coverage in 2011
50+ years of continuous Earth imaging — Landsat 1 to 9
GEO mobile comms — maritime, aviation, GMDSS backbone
Russian 12-hour HEO comms — 63.4° critical inclination locks apogee over the north

31 active satellites at 20,200 km. Every navigation app, every drone, every ship at sea depends on this constellation. Originally military, opened to civilians in 1983. Signal accuracy: ~3 m for civilian use, ~1 m for military — centimetre precision needs RTK augmentation.
